concrete_changes.before: The ancients knew better. Their debugging practices were far more radical, far more embodied, and — if we are being honest — far more effective.
concrete_changes.after: The ancient practices make the debugging joke uncomfortable. An intervention can restore a city's story about itself while doing terrible things to the person selected to carry that story.

concrete_changes.before: This is garbage collection. Specifically, it is a mark-and-sweep algorithm.
concrete_changes.after: Mark-and-sweep is my analogy for this assignment and expulsion. It should make the violence harder to overlook, not turn a person into disposable memory.

concrete_changes.before: The Hebrew tradition refined this into the Yom Kippur protocol, which is more sophisticated.
concrete_changes.after: The Yom Kippur account offers a separate ritual comparison.

concrete_changes.before: This is not mythology. This is a role specification for a debugging agent.
concrete_changes.after: Read through the debugger comparison, these mythic figures give the boundary-crossing role a face.

concrete_changes.before: The caduceus — the staff of Hermes with two intertwined serpents — is the original debugging symbol.
concrete_changes.after: I borrow the caduceus — the staff of Hermes with two intertwined serpents — as a debugging image.

concrete_changes.before: The technique is identical. Only the runtime differs.
concrete_changes.after: The comparison connects levels of a system. It does not establish that entrails can diagnose a city the way a trace can expose a software call.

concrete_changes.before: The vocabulary has changed. The architecture has not.
concrete_changes.after: The recurring question is what a scheduled gathering makes visible, and what it permits a group to ignore.

concrete_changes.before: The ancient debugging practices were not primitive precursors to modern programming. They were sophisticated interventions in the most complex runtime environment known to exist: human consciousness.
concrete_changes.after: Ancient ritual and modern programming meet here through comparison. Their histories, purposes and consequences remain different.

concrete_changes.before: The runtime is still sacred. The debugging is still necessary. And the first step is still the same one the ancients took: admit that the system is not running as designed, sit down with the stack trace, and start reading.
concrete_changes.after: The stack trace becomes more interesting when it includes the person who pays for the fix. That question survives the joke about the moth.

concrete_changes.before: They understood that the bug is not an external intruder. The bug is a systemic condition that requires systemic intervention. And sometimes, that intervention meant physically throwing someone out of the city.
concrete_changes.after: The software image makes the condition systemic. The historical question is harder: what did the expulsion accomplish, and who bore its cost?
